claims.text: A hybrid strategy combining first-principles or CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling with targeted DSC and dilatometry can determine melting and liquid-phase properties across a wide range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Using only minimal DSC and in-situ dilatometry trials is sufficient to refine model parameters for each alloy composition.
The proposed calibration procedure can improve predictions of melting transitions and liquid-phase properties.
DSC heating rates of 5–20 K/min capture melting transitions accurately.
Multiple principal elements produce entropic stabilization in high-entropy alloys.
Entropic stabilization in high-entropy alloys results in sloped free-energy surfaces.
These free-energy surfaces can be screened by combining mixing-enthalpy and configurational-entropy models with partial experimental data.
Local chemical and topological disorder in multi-principal-element alloys modifies lattice vibrational entropy.
Local chemical and topological disorder in multi-principal-element alloys modifies enthalpy.
Combining thermodynamic modeling with direct thermal and volumetric measurements can capture disorder-related thermodynamics sufficiently to predict bulk melting behavior and liquid-phase stability.
The strategy will predict melting temperatures to within ±10 K.
The strategy will predict enthalpies of fusion to within ±5%.
The strategy will predict entropies of fusion to within ±5%.
The strategy will determine volume changes upon melting with less than 5% deviation from direct experimental measurements.
The stated prediction performance applies to multi-principal-element alloys at or near equiatomic compositions.
Existing empirical correlations or unrefined databases often deviate by 20–30% for melting points and fusion parameters of compositionally complex high-entropy alloys.
The approach is most applicable to single-phase or near-single-phase, minimally segregated, equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Multiphase or metastable high-entropy-alloy compositions may produce larger prediction uncertainties.
Oxidation, partial reactions, and database extrapolation beyond characterized composition ranges may cause anomalous model predictions.
The approach is invalidated if more than half of at least 10 tested alloys exceed either ±10% fusion-enthalpy error or ±10 K melting-temperature error.
